| [THEORY-028](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-028.md) v2 | The expected bias of any data-dependent choice, and the expected generalisation error of any learning algorithm, is at most √(2σ²·I) for σ-subgaussian losses, where I is the information the output carries about the data | Russo & Zou (2015), [LIT-356](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-356.md), Prop. 1: \|E[φ_T − µ_T]\| ≤ σ√(2·I(T;φ)) for any selection T among σ-sub-Gaussian statistics. Xu & Raginsky (2017), [LIT-347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-347.md), Thm 1: \|gen\| ≤ √(2σ²·I(S;W)/n) for any algorithm P_{W\|S}. Both proofs rest on Donsker–Varadhan and were checked by the readers. The bound is in expectation only. It is vacuous for deterministic learners on continuous hypotheses, where I(S;W) is infinite, and for any real network when I is bounded by counting bits. It is tight only for Gaussian argmax and threshold selection. | Active |
| [THEORY-031](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-031.md) | The likelihood-ratio detector is optimal under the payoff, Neyman–Pearson and posterior criteria, which differ only in its threshold, so performance is an ROC and the criterion a point on it; d′ is criterion-free only for equal-variance normal signal and noise | Peterson & Birdsall (1953), [LIT-364](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-364.md) — the threshold on ℓ = f_SN/f_N is optimal for expected value and at fixed false-alarm rate, and the two optimum families coincide (Part I Thms 1–7). The ROC's slope equals the threshold (Thm 8). Tanner & Swets (1954), [LIT-368](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-368.md), carry this over to the human observer as d′ plus a criterion. Stanislaw & Todorov (1999), [LIT-367](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-367.md), state that d′ varies with the criterion unless the variances are equal. The separation of sensitivity from bias is a property of the model, not of the data. | Active |
| [THEORY-066](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-066.md) | A Markov-blanket partition is defined relative to a chosen internal set, so a graph has one around almost any set of nodes, and the formalism alone does not say which set is the system | The formal core of Bruineberg et al.'s critique ([LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md), C4 in [NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)). In a directed acyclic graph the blanket of a node set A is its parents, children and the children's other parents, and A is conditionally independent of everything outside A and its blanket. That holds for every A, so any set whose blanket leaves something outside gets a valid internal, blanket and external partition. Having a blanket therefore picks out no set. In Friston's soup ([LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md)) the set was picked by spectral clustering with k = 8, not by the blanket. Active because it is a short derivation that anyone can check. It covers graphical (Pearl) blankets and the 2013 procedure. It does not cover the later sparse-coupling definitions at nonequilibrium steady state, which the record has not read. | Active |
| [THEORY-068](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md) | In a two-alternative choice made by two competing leaky accumulators, the decision is optimal only when leak and mutual inhibition balance, so that the network integrates the difference of the evidence without loss; imbalance bounds accuracy at any fixed time and weights early or late evidence | Bogacz et al. ([LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md)) prove that the pure drift diffusion model is the continuum limit of the sequential probability ratio test, and so the optimal two-choice decider, and that the linearised Usher–McClelland network reduces to it exactly when leak equals inhibition (and, for free response, when both are also large). Usher and McClelland ([LIT-565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-565.md)) derived the difference of the two units as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β: K ≠ 0 caps accuracy, leak-dominant weights late evidence and inhibition-dominant early. Active because the core is derivation, checkable on paper. What it does not say: that brains are balanced, that the result carries to more than two options or to non-stationary evidence, or that the primacy and recency seen in six participants are explained by it. | Active |
| [THEORY-073](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-073.md) | A Markov blanket does not individuate a system: where it falls is fixed by modelling choices made before it is found, so it presupposes the boundary it is used to find, and it cannot represent a boundary the system produces | Bruineberg et al. ([LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md)) and Raja et al. ([LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md)) argue, by different routes, that the Markov blanket of the free-energy literature is placed and not found. The formal core is [THEORY-066](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-066.md): the partition takes the internal set as input. This account adds what the critiques show about practice. In Friston's soup ([LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md)) the graph was built from one kind of coupling and steady state was assumed when the run stopped. In published applications the blanket sits wherever the model needs it: in the receptors of a brain, the membrane of a bacillus, the beam joining two pendulums. The formalism also gives the same description to a membrane the cell makes and a beam nobody's states make. So the blanket presupposes the boundary it is offered as the criterion of. Proposed: the argument is conceptual, and the later steady-state definitions have not been read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-079](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-079.md) v2 | Bayesian model reduction under the Laplace approximation prices the reductions of a singular parent model with a Gaussian Occam factor, so its free-energy differences can be wrong by a term that grows with log n | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. BMR's closed form (Friston & Penny, [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 9; Friston, Parr & Zeidman, [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md), Eq. 11) charges a reduction through log-determinants of Gaussian precisions, which is MacKay's regular Occam factor. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), says that models with hierarchical layers or hidden variables are singular, that no normal distribution approximates their posterior, and that their free energy grows as λ log n. BMR is applied to exactly such models: mixtures, hierarchical empirical Bayes and latent states. Neither literature cites the other. The exact identity is untouched ([THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md)). The claim is about its Laplace form, and a test on reduced-rank regression would settle it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md) v2 | The evidence of any model formed from a full model by changing only its prior is the full evidence times the full posterior expectation of the prior ratio, so the Savage–Dickey ratio is its point-mass case and choosing which parameters to keep is evidence maximisation over the prior | Friston & Penny (2011), [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 3: if models share a likelihood and differ only in priors nested inside a full prior, then p(y\|m_i) = p(y\|m_F)·E_{p(θ\|y,m_F)}[p_i(θ)/p_F(θ)]. Their Eq. 6 is the point-mass case, the Savage–Dickey ratio that Wagenmakers et al. (2010), [LIT-609](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-609.md), derive from the other end, and that Dickey (1971), LIT-610, stated in this form for any continuous likelihood. Friston, Parr & Zeidman, [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md), restate it for any new prior and give conjugate closed forms. Active because the identity is three lines of Bayes' rule that anyone can check. The two Savage–Dickey conditions turn out to be the same condition. The identity is exact. Its Laplace and variational forms are only as good as the full posterior, and with no constraint on the prior family the optimum is maximum likelihood. | Active |
| [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md) | The Bayesian complexity penalty grows as (d/2) log n in a regular model, where the curvature at the optimum sets the Occam factor, and as λ log n in a singular one, where λ is the real log canonical threshold and falls below d/2 when the prior is positive on the optimal set | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), writes the evidence as best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible volume, which under a Gaussian approximation is P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A. When the likelihood dominates, det A grows as n^d, so the penalty is (d/2) log n. Watanabe's WBIC paper, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), recovers that case (Lemma 3, Theorem 5) and states what replaces it when the Fisher information is degenerate at the optimum: λ log n − (m − 1) log log n, with λ the RLCT (Theorem 2). The regular half is derived. The singular half is a theorem the record holds only as cited, so this is Proposed. The volume reading of λ is in Watanabe's book, which is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-155](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-155.md) | Iterated learning by Bayesian agents who sample from the posterior converges to the shared prior | Griffiths & Kalish (2007), [LIT-769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-769.md), read in [NOTE-599](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-599.md): a chain of learners who share a prior and each sample a hypothesis from their posterior is a Gibbs sampler, so the probability a learner holds a hypothesis converges to its prior probability, whatever the amount of data passed on; with MAP learners the outcome centres on the prior's mode but depends on data amount and noise, and can amplify weak biases. It is a theorem about an idealized chain. It does not say human chains reach the prior, and Kirby, Cornish & Smith's laboratory chains, [LIT-771](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-771.md), are consistent with it without testing it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-157](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-157.md) | The classical theorems on sufficient statistics need only the copy/discard structure of Markov kernels: Basu's theorem holds in every Markov category, and Fisher–Neyman and Bahadur need only strict positivity, not the existence of conditional distributions | Fritz (2020), [LIT-772](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-772.md), read in [NOTE-588](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-588.md), Theorems 14.5, 15.8 and 16.3 with the definitions of Sections 13–15. Sufficiency, completeness and ancillarity are stated with copy, discard, composition and almost-sure equality alone. Basu's theorem follows with no further axiom; Fisher–Neyman and Bahadur use strict positivity, which Stoch has although it lacks regular conditionals. The match with the classical theorems is shown in FinStoch (Fisher–Neyman) and through bounded completeness in Stoch (Basu), not for measure-theoretic Fisher–Neyman. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-158](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-158.md) | In a Markov process, an observable commutes with the generator exactly when its mean and variance are both conserved in every state; on a finite state space this means it is constant on each connected component of the transition graph, so a conserved mean alone does not give a symmetry | Baez & Fong (2013), [LIT-773](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-773.md), read in [NOTE-598](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-598.md): Theorem 1 (finite state space, four equivalent conditions) and Theorems 2–3 (σ-finite measure spaces, without the component form). Unlike quantum mechanics, where a mean conserved in every state already implies commutation, a Markov process can conserve the mean of an observable it does not commute with. The theorem covers diagonal observables only; it says nothing about symmetries that permute states. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-166](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-166.md) | Survey question-order effects leave the probability of giving the same answer to both questions unchanged, as a projection model predicts, and this regularity does not by itself favour quantum over classical probability | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer (2014), [LIT-795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-795.md), on the QQ equality derived in [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md): across 66 unselected Pew surveys, question order shifts the answers (p = 0.0004) but not the probability that the two answers agree (p = 0.4625). The Lüders projection model predicts this without parameters. The authors concede that a classical model can be built to satisfy the equality, and [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) shows that data meeting it are noncontextual, so it is evidence for a constraint on order effects, not for nonclassical probability or contextuality. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-172](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-172.md) | Listeners in simple reference games interpret an utterance by inverting a model of a speaker who chooses among alternatives by informativeness, so the interpretation of a fixed form depends on what else the speaker could have said | Frank & Goodman (2012), [LIT-821](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-821.md), read in [NOTE-634](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-634.md): a parameter-free Bayesian listener inverting a size-principle speaker, with a measured salience prior, predicts mean listener bets at r = .99; Bergen, Goodman & Levy (2012), [LIT-809](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-809.md), read in [NOTE-613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-613.md): people draw specificity and Horn implicatures among novel signals, and lexical uncertainty lets the same recursion derive Horn's mapping; Goodman & Frank (2016), [LIT-816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-816.md), states the framework. | [THEORY-177](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-177.md) | In a binary cyclic system, the Contextuality-by-Default measure of signalling is twice the least total direct influence of context that any canonical causal model of the data must contain, and each content's share is the total-variation distance between its marginals | Wang, Sadrzadeh, Abramsky & Cervantes (2021), [LIT-851](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-851.md), Proposition 1. It joins CbD's maximal couplings ([LIT-777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-777.md), Theorem 3.3) to Jones's 2019 correspondence between couplings and canonical models, which is quoted, not proved. | [THEORY-203](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-203.md) | In data generated by a random hierarchical grammar, the tokens that Bayes-optimal noising and denoising changes do so in blocks set by the depth of the latent that changed, and the block size, measured as the correlation length of the changes, diverges at the noise threshold where the top-level class is lost, as a power of the distance to it whose exponent is log(branching) over log(slope of the level-to-level belief map at its unstable fixed point); a Gaussian field with power-law spectrum has instead a correlation length of changes that grows with noise to the end of the process | Sclocchi, Favero, Levi and Wyart (2024; ICLR 2025), [LIT-886](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-886.md): an annealed mean-field computation of the pair statistics of token changes in the Random Hierarchy Model, a scaling argument for the exponent, and one data collapse against exact BP at v = 32, m = 8, s = 2. | [THEORY-215](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-215.md) | A Hawkes process with a Lipschitz rate function and signed kernels has a unique stationary regime, which suitably started versions approach, when the Lipschitz-weighted absolute kernel mass is below one (a spectral radius below one, for a network) or when the rate is bounded | Brémaud and Massoulié (1996), [LIT-1035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1035.md), read in [NOTE-728](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-728.md): Theorems 1, 2, 7 and 8, proved. Inhibition is allowed because the conditions use \|h\|. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the kernels are fixed in time; uniqueness is among solutions with finite mean intensity. In the linear excitatory case the condition is the branching ratio below one, but in the nonlinear signed case the spectral-radius quantity is a bound, not a branching ratio, and a bounded rate needs no bound on the kernels at all. Nothing is proved about cascade sizes or about what happens past the threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-247](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-247.md) | For finite labelled Markov chains, the discounted bisimulation metric is a bicausal optimal-transport distance, and it equals the value of a finite linear program over occupancy couplings | Calo, Jonsson, Neu, Schwartz & Segovia-Aguas (2024), [LIT-962](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-962.md), read in [NOTE-757](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-757.md). For finite action-free chains with real labels r and discount γ, the bisimulation metric's fixed-point equation is the Bellman equation of transport over bicausal couplings with cost (1−γ)\|r(x)−r(y)\|, so the two coincide. The transport cost equals 1/(1−γ) times the minimum of a linear objective over occupancy couplings, under flow and coherence constraints (Lemma 1, Theorem 1). It says nothing of systems with actions. Its link to trace distance is one-way and second-hand. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-256](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-256.md) | When a sequence generator's latent dynamics factor as a tensor product, its predictive state embeds losslessly and linearly in orthogonal per-factor subspaces of total dimension Σ(d_n − 1); small transformers trained by next-token prediction on such processes settle near that dimension in approximately orthogonal subspaces, and reach it first even when noise makes it lossy | Shai et al. (2026), [LIT-986](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-986.md), read in [NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md). The lossless embedding is an elementary theorem (Prop. 2.2, Thm 2.3, App. A). The rest is experiment on five synthetic factors: about 10 effective dimensions against 242 for the joint state, approximate orthogonality in the first two components, and under token noise a collapse to the factored form before expansion. It does not show that the preference is architectural rather than a feature of training, a question the paper leaves open, and it varies neither the objective nor the data domain. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-280](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-280.md) | The bisimulation metric between two finite Markov chains can be estimated from sampled transitions without a transition model, to accuracy ε with a number of samples polynomial in the state-space sizes and 1/ε² | Calo, Jonsson, Neu, Schwartz & Segovia-Aguas (2025), [LIT-948](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-948.md), read in [NOTE-763](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-763.md). Bicausal occupancy couplings are characterised by constraints that use only each chain's sampled occupancy measure over consecutive state pairs. A stochastic primal-dual method on them gets an ε-accurate estimate with probability 1−δ from O((\|X\|\|Y\|(\|X\|+\|Y\|) + (\|X\|+\|Y\|)log(1/δ))/((1−γ)²ε²)) independent samples per chain. The states must be observed and enumerable, the cost known, and the samples drawn with restarts. A single running stream and latent states are outside it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-289](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-289.md) | When each round of a fixed-design linear regression is refit to labels generated by the previous fit, keeping every earlier round's data bounds the test error at π²/6 times the first fit's, where replacing the data makes it grow linearly in the number of rounds | Gerstgrasser, Schaeffer, Dey et al. (2024), [LIT-971](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-971.md), read in [NOTE-815](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-815.md), Theorems 1–2 extending Dohmatob et al.'s replace result. Proved for ridgeless OLS with isotropic Gaussian features, the real covariates reused every round and only labels regenerated. The error is bounded, not constant: it rises every round towards its limit, and every model remains a noisier copy of the first. Small language and diffusion models behave alike over five to eight rounds; a VAE's error still rises. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-305](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-305.md) | SimCLR's InfoNCE loss, over all n objects with a Gaussian kernel on the unit sphere, equals a graph-Laplacian quadratic form on the augmentation matrix plus the log of InfoNCE's normalizers, which is spectral clustering only in a sense that admits any regularizer and does not make the minimizer the Laplacian's eigenvectors | Tan, Zhang, Yang & Yuan (2023, ICLR 2024), [LIT-227](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-227.md), read in [NOTE-846](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-846.md): Theorem 3.1 and its proof (App. A), Lemma 2.5 and Definition 2.7. The identity between objectives is exact on a finite object set with symmetric π. The paper's "spectral clustering" is any Laplacian form plus any regularizer; it names no minimizer and no population optimum, so it supports neither an eigenvector reading of InfoNCE nor the density-ratio optimum of [THEORY-001](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-001.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-306](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-306.md) | Volume-maximizing joint-embedding objectives carry a prior toward equal-sized clusters, explicit in MSN and SwAV and derived for VICReg only through a reduction to K-means, and with mini-batches of two to eight classes they lose semantic transfer while MAE and data2vec do not | Assran et al. (2022), [LIT-231](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-231.md), §§3–5 and Appendix C, read in [NOTE-850](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-850.md). The prior is explicit in MSN's loss (a KL to uniform over mean cluster assignments) and in SwAV's equipartition constraint. For VICReg it rests on an informal reduction of a simplified loss to K-means and on K-means's cited tendency to equal clusters, and for SimCLR on a cited equivalence. | [THEORY-313](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-313.md) | With a kernel normalised to k(x,x) = 1, the covariance operator of a distribution is a density operator, and its quantum relative entropy is a lower bound on the Kullback–Leibler divergence that is tight only for an orthonormal, hence discrete, embedding, lies above the KL of the kernel-smoothed distributions, and on the torus is within O(σ²) of KL as the bandwidth σ shrinks | Bach (2022), [LIT-255](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-255.md), read in [NOTE-837](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-837.md). Σ_p = ∫ϕϕ* dp is uncentred and unit-trace, so p ↦ Σ_p maps distributions to quantum states, and D(p̃‖q̃) ≤ D(Σ_p‖Σ_q) ≤ D(p‖q) (Proposition 4(d), Eq. 8). The upper bound is joint convexity, with equality only if k(x,y) = 0 for x ≠ y. The lower bound is monotonicity under a measurement whose outcome law is p smoothed by h(x,y) = ⟨ϕ(x), Σ^{−1/2}ϕ(y)⟩². The O(σ²) gap is shown only for translation-invariant kernels on the torus with Lipschitz densities. It does not cover centred kernels, or similarity measures that compare Gram matrices of representations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-336](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-336.md) | An ideal observer is optimal relative to the information it is given, so a constrained ideal is the optimal decoder of a degraded input, not a restricted decoder of the full one; comparing real observers with ideals taken at successive stages of the visual system places losses by stage, and in early-vision tasks human performance is reported to parallel the retinal-stage ideal across conditions while falling well below it | Geisler (2011), [LIT-1055](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1055.md), read in [NOTE-870](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-870.md). A review that defines the ideal observer as optimal "given the available information and any specified constraints", and writes it as an expected-utility argmax over the posterior given the stimulus S or a constrained representation Z = g(S;θ). Constraints are added one at a time (optics, receptor sampling and noise, ganglion-cell summation), and human performance that parallels the retinal-stage ideal while falling below it is read as loss in central factors. The empirical parts are the review's account of studies the record has not read. The review gives no formula for efficiency and no notion of an optimum over a restricted class of computations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-339](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-339.md) | People's answers to a probability query depend on their own answers to an earlier query whose result it can use: a person's sub-answer predicts their later answer only when asked first, and a bias induced in a first judgment carries into a second only when the two share part of a hypothesis space, so reuse carries the earlier error with it; that reuse saves computation rests on one small response-time study and one secondary-task result | Dasgupta, Schulz, Goodman and Gershman (2018), [LIT-1074](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1074.md), read in [NOTE-875](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-875.md); Gershman and Goodman (2014), [LIT-1056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1056.md), read in [NOTE-886](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-886.md); Dasgupta and Gershman (2021), [LIT-1077](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1077.md), read in [NOTE-865](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-865.md). In five small online experiments, an earlier answer shapes a later one only when the later query can use it, and errors in the first carry into the second. The authors call this amortized inference, reuse of past computation bought at a cost in bias. The speed benefit is shown once (median log-RT facilitation, n ≈ 50 per order) and otherwise assumed; storage and retrieval are free in the models; the 2021 review adds stale cached values from the planning literature, second-hand. No paper prices when reuse pays or touches stores outside the head. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-349](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-349.md) | For binary outcomes and a fixed representation of individuals, a predictor can pass every test in a bounded class without being close to nature: outcome indistinguishability to tests that see the sampled prediction is equivalent, with stated losses, to multicalibration over a closely related class of sets, a predictor meeting it exists at size polynomial in the tests' size and the tolerance whatever nature's complexity, and learning one is as hard as weak agnostic learning of the class | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md), and Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md), read in [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md). A predictor is outcome indistinguishable relative to a class of distinguishers when none can tell nature's outcomes from outcomes drawn from the predictor, up to ε. With no access or sample access to the predictor this is equivalent to multi-accuracy or multicalibration over closely related classes, and a predictor meeting it exists at size O(s/ε²) (O(s/α⁴γ) for multicalibration), independent of nature. Learning a multicalibrated predictor is equivalent to weak agnostic learning of the class. Adequacy here is relative to the class, the outcome and the features, and is not unique; it is not closeness to the truth, and the papers say nothing about signal detection. | Active |
| [THEORY-354](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-354.md) | An observer's power to refute a predictor depends on its access to the predictor as well as on its budget: against tests that see only the sampled prediction a predictor of size O(s/ε²) always passes, but if fine-grained clique counting is hard, or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some cheap tests that may query the predictor adaptively pass only predictors about as costly as nature's own | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md). Against sample-access distinguishers of size s an outcome-indistinguishable predictor of size O(s/ε²) always exists. Against oracle-access distinguishers, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, there are natures and polynomially many cheap distinguishers such that no predictor much cheaper than nature is indistinguishable. Non-adaptive queries add little; the power comes from adaptive queries. The results are conditional and asymptotic, with upper and lower bounds in different parameterisations; they say nothing about human observers or about which access a real auditor has. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. Theorem 1: for n fixed data points and an independent query, var(d^p / E[d^p]) → 0 implies P[DMAX ≤ (1+ε)DMIN] → 1 for every ε > 0. The index m is arbitrary, so dimension enters only through the workload's distance distributions. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
